title: 21 Anti-rhodococcal antibodies are negatively correlated with serum concentration of cortisol in newborn foals
content:
Abstract
Rhodococcus equi (R equi) is a Gram-positive facultative intracellular pathogen known to cause a severe form of pneumonia in foals. Virulent strains of R equi express virulence-associated protein A (VapA), which plays a critical role in enabling the bacterium to replicate within macrophages and contribute to disease pathogenesis. As antibodies targeting rhodococcal VapA appear to convey protection, it is important to identify factors that affect the quantity and/or activity of anti-R equi antibodies. We hypothesized that lower serum concentrations of cortisol would be associated with increased relative activities of immunoglobulin sub-isotypes (IgG1 and IgG4/7) against VapA in newborn foals. Archived serum samples from 356 foals (1-2 d of age; sex recorded on 327 Thoroughbred foals: 169 males and 158 females) from 13 New York farms were used (Bettencourt et al., 2023, Amer. J. Vet. Res. 85(3), ajvr.23.08.0180). Aliquots of serum that had not been thawed were tested by ELISA for relative activities against VapA of IgG1 and IgG4/7 sub-isotypes and were expressed as a percentage of the positive control. Serum concentration of cortisol was determined by RIA. The association of individual or multiple independent variables was examined using linear mixed-effects modeling in R using the nlme package with farm modeled as a random effect to account for clustering of observations within farms. Confidence intervals were estimated using maximum-likelihood methods. Activities of IgG1 and IgG4/7 recognizing VapA did not differ between males and females. Activity of IgG1 ranged from < 0.1% to 120.5% of the positive control (mean, 12.7%; SD, 18.0%; median, 6.7%; 25th percentile, 2.0%), and activity of IgG4/7 ranged from < 0.1% to 173.2% of the positive control (mean, 17.2%; SD 24.8%; median, 8.2%; 25th percentile, 2.7%). Serum cortisol ranged from 5.7 to 96.2 ng/mL and did not differ between males (22.0 ± 0.9 ng/mL) and females (21.6 ± 1 ng/mL). Foals were separated into quartiles based on IgG1 and IgG4/7 activity. Values of anti-VapA IgG1 activity were significantly and negatively associated with serum cortisol concentration. Specifically, foals in the 2 lower quartiles of IgG1 had greater cortisol concentration than foals in the 2 higher quartiles of IgG1 activity (P ≤ 0.05). Similarly, foals in the two lower quartiles of IgG4/7 had greater serum cortisol concentration than foals in the highest quartile of IgG4/7 activity (P ≤ 0.05). Negative Pearson correlation coefficients characterized the association (P ≤ 0.05) of serum cortisol with levels of IgG1 (r = −0.14) and IgG4/7 (r = −0.15) activity against VapA. These observations suggest that an elevated serum concentration of cortisol in newborn foals may modulate the presence of anti-rhodococcal antibodies. An impact of this relationship on foal health remains to be determined.
